prompt_free_text:
This paper studies hybrid reinforcement learning in linear MDPs, with both an online-to-offline PAC objective and an offline-to-online regret objective. The central claim is that hybrid RL can provably improve over the best-known offline-only or online-only guarantees without relying on single-policy concentrability, extending prior positive results from the tabular setting to linear function approximation. The paper proposes two algorithms: RAPPEL, which uses reward-agnostic exploration to augment offline data and then runs pessimistic offline RL, and HYRULE, which warm-starts an optimistic online RL algorithm using offline data. The main theoretical results are an error bound for RAPPEL and a regret bound for HYRULE, both expressed through a partition of the feature space into “offline-covered” and “online-needing-exploration” components, with dependence on partial coverage quantities rather than global concentrability.

Overall, I think the paper addresses an important and timely question, and the high-level message is interesting: hybrid RL can indeed beat the barriers suggested by pure offline or pure online learning in linear MDPs, at least under the paper’s partition-based characterization. The work is ambitious in that it treats both PAC and regret settings, and it appears to combine several recent technical ingredients in a nontrivial way. The paper is also well motivated, and the distinction between online-to-offline and offline-to-online approaches is useful conceptually. That said, I have substantial reservations about the sharpness and clarity of some assumptions, the practical meaning of the guarantees, and the extent to which the claimed “barrier breaking” is fully convincing in the strongest sense suggested by the title. My overall assessment is positive but cautious.

The strongest aspect of the paper is its scope and positioning. Prior work had either focused on tabular settings for genuine improvements, or on linear/general function approximation without such improvements or under stronger assumptions. This paper fills a meaningful gap by giving computationally efficient algorithms in linear MDPs for both PAC and regret formulations. The partition-based analysis, separating the state-action-feature space into an offline-covered part and an online-explored part, is a natural and potentially powerful lens. The resulting bounds interpolate between offline and online contributions and can be strictly better than pure offline or pure online rates when the partition is favorable. This is a compelling conceptual contribution.

The RAPPEL result is particularly interesting because it leverages reward-agnostic exploration and then invokes a strong offline RL guarantee on the combined dataset. The first inequality in Theorem 1 is clean and appealing: adding online exploration can only improve the covariance relative to offline-only learning, so the instance-dependent offline error term improves monotonically. This is a nice way to formalize the benefit of hybridization. The comparison to Wagenmaker and Pacchiano is also meaningful, especially the improved horizon dependence. Likewise, HYRULE gives a regret guarantee that adapts to the best partition even though the algorithm itself is partition-unaware, which is a desirable property.

I also appreciate that the paper is explicit about limitations and open problems. In particular, the discussion acknowledges that the horizon dependence is still not fully optimal in the general linear case, that the burn-in/sample lower-order requirements are large, and that the two algorithms separately improve offline-only and online-only baselines rather than a single algorithm simultaneously improving both. This honesty improves the credibility of the work.

That said, my main concern is that several of the headline claims are stronger than what the technical results seem to fully support. The title says “breaks sample size barriers,” and the abstract suggests improvements over optimal sample complexity in offline RL and online RL “regardless of the quality of the behavior policy.” But the actual guarantees depend on a partition and on quantities such as c_off(X_off) and d_on, and for RAPPEL also on Assumption 2 and the exploration cost N*(tau). In the worst case, these quantities may not yield a meaningful improvement beyond standard rates, and the burn-in/sample requirements can be enormous. So the paper does show the possibility of improvement and no-worse-than behavior under its framework, but the title and abstract read closer to a universal barrier-breaking theorem than what is actually established. I would encourage the authors to moderate the framing and be more precise about the conditional nature of the gains.

A second major concern is the role and interpretation of Assumption 2 for RAPPEL. The paper presents it as a projected full-rank explorability condition and argues that it is mild or achievable via feature transformation. However, this deserves much more careful treatment. If the feature map is transformed using the covariance of the offline dataset, then the resulting representation and the meaning of the linear MDP assumption may change in subtle ways. More importantly, saying that one can project onto the nonzero singular space of observed offline features does not obviously imply that the online partition is explorable in the sense required for every partition. The assumption quantifies over any partition and requires existence of a policy whose projected covariance has full rank on the online subspace at every stage. This is a fairly strong structural assumption about the MDP and feature map, and I do not think the current discussion adequately justifies calling it mild. Since RAPPEL’s guarantee depends critically on OPTCOV and this assumption, the paper should either strengthen the justification, weaken the claim, or provide concrete examples/counterexamples clarifying when the assumption holds.

Relatedly, Lemma 1 claims that for any partition, c_on(X_on) <= d_on, and that there exists at least one partition with c_off(X_off)=O(d). These are important structural statements, but from the summary alone they seem surprisingly strong. In particular, a universal upper bound c_on <= d_on independent of MDP dynamics is not intuitive unless the definition of c_on and the linear MDP structure impose very special geometry. Since these lemmas are central to the claimed improvements, the paper should make their intuition much more transparent in the main text. As written, the reader is asked to accept a very favorable structural fact with little explanation.

A third concern is the practical significance of the asymptotic improvements given the very large lower-order requirements. Theorem 2 requires N_on, N_off = \tilde{\Omega}(d^{13} H^{14}), which is extremely large. Even if this is inherited from prior analyses plus new truncation arguments, it substantially weakens the practical meaning of the regret result. Similarly, Theorem 1 requires N to exceed a maximum involving N*(tau) and a polynomial in d, H, c_off, etc., and the dependence on alpha_on and alpha_off is somewhat opaque. If the paper’s main message is that hybrid RL can beat sample barriers, then the authors should more clearly separate asymptotic leading-term improvements from the potentially prohibitive pre-asymptotic regime. Right now, the theoretical message is interesting, but the practical sample-efficiency implications are much less clear.

I also found some aspects of the theorem statements and comparisons difficult to parse. For RAPPEL, Theorem 1 gives two different upper bounds inside a minimum, one with H^4 and one with H^3 but worse dependence on c_off and d_on. The discussion then emphasizes H^3 dependence, but the actual tradeoff is more nuanced. It would help to explicitly state in which regimes each term dominates and whether the H^3 term is genuinely preferable in realistic parameter ranges. Similarly, the comparison to offline-only minimax-optimal bounds is somewhat delicate: the paper compares to an instance-dependent offline bound and also to a worst-case bound under a well-covered assumption. These are not directly interchangeable, and the narrative occasionally blurs the distinction.

For HYRULE, the regret bound scales as sqrt(c_off(X_off)^2 d H^3 N_on^2 / N_off) + sqrt(d_on d H^3 N_on). The first term is unusual because of the N_on^2 / N_off factor inside the square root, i.e. linear in N_on / sqrt(N_off). This means the offline benefit can vanish unless N_off is much larger than N_on. The paper does mention this, but the practical interpretation should be more explicit. In particular, the claim that the result “improves upon the online-only minimax optimal bound” is true in some regimes but not uniformly compelling unless N_off is sufficiently large. Again, the framing should be more careful.

The experimental section is useful as a sanity check, but it is not strong enough to substantiate the breadth of the theoretical claims. The experiments are limited to a scaled-down Tetris environment with projected one-hot features and relatively small trial counts. More importantly, the implementations do not exactly match the theory: the paper substitutes LSVI-UCB for FORCE inside OPTCOV and LinPEVI-ADV for LinPEVI-ADV+, and for Algorithm 2 it implements LSVI-UCB++ “as-is.” This is understandable from an engineering standpoint, but it weakens the empirical support for the specific algorithms analyzed. The experiments show that warm-starting helps and that reward-agnostic exploration can improve coverage, but they do not really validate the partition-based theory or the claimed dependence on c_off and d_on. I would not hold this too strongly against a theory paper, but the paper should be more explicit that the experiments are illustrative rather than validating the exact theoretical algorithms.

There are also several presentation issues that should be improved. The paper is generally readable, but some notation is overloaded or introduced too quickly. The partition notation is central, yet the operational meaning of choosing a partition is not always clear. For RAPPEL, the user apparently needs to choose a tolerance related to d_on, but the partition itself is not algorithmically constructed. This raises a conceptual gap between the existential theorem statement and the actual algorithm deployment. If the guarantee is “for every partition,” but the algorithm only uses a tolerance and not an explicit partition, then the paper should explain more concretely how the analysis maps to practice. For HYRULE, the partition is purely analytical, which is elegant, but then the infimum over partitions in Theorem 2 should be discussed more intuitively.

I also noticed a number of minor issues: some typographical errors, duplicated commas in citations, inconsistent notation, and a few places where the prose is rough. The footnote about a typo in He et al. is useful, but it should be handled carefully and perhaps moved to an appendix if space is tight. Table 2 is ambitious but dense; it would benefit from a clearer explanation of what is being compared and under what assumptions. The statement “there always exists a partition such that c_off(X_off), d_on <= d” is true but not very informative by itself, since trivial partitions may satisfy it without yielding strong gains.

My recommendation would depend heavily on the conference’s standards for theory papers. On the positive side, the paper tackles an important open direction, gives nontrivial algorithms and analyses, and appears to improve the state of the art in hybrid RL for linear MDPs. On the negative side, some assumptions and claims need sharper qualification, the practical significance is limited by very large polynomial requirements, and the empirical section is only lightly supportive. If the proofs are correct, I view this as a meaningful contribution, but not yet a fully polished or definitive one.

The most important revisions I would ask for are the following. First, clarify and possibly soften the main claims in the title, abstract, and introduction so they accurately reflect that the improvements are conditional on partition-dependent quantities and, for RAPPEL, on an explorability assumption and exploration cost. Second, substantially strengthen the discussion of Assumption 2 and Lemma 1, including intuition, examples where they hold, and examples where they may fail or be nontrivial. Third, improve the interpretation of the bounds by explicitly discussing the regimes in which hybrid gains are substantial versus negligible, especially for HYRULE’s N_on^2 / N_off dependence. Fourth, make clearer which parts of the empirical study correspond exactly to the analyzed algorithms and which are proxies. Fifth, if possible, add a concise comparison table or paragraph that distinguishes instance-dependent improvements, worst-case improvements, and asymptotic versus pre-asymptotic requirements.

In summary, I find the paper technically interesting and potentially impactful, especially because it extends genuine hybrid-RL improvements beyond the tabular setting and covers both PAC and regret formulations. However, I also think the current presentation overstates the universality of the result, and some assumptions and tradeoffs need much clearer exposition. With stronger qualification of claims and improved clarity around the structural assumptions and regimes of benefit, this could become a strong theory paper.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies hybrid reinforcement learning in episodic linear MDPs, where an agent has both an offline dataset and the ability to collect online data. It proposes two computationally efficient algorithms: RAPPEL, an online-to-offline method that uses reward-agnostic exploration (via OPTCOV) to augment offline data before running a pessimistic offline RL solver; and HYRULE, an offline-to-online method that warm-starts a regret-minimizing online RL algorithm using offline data. The main claims are that, without assuming single-policy concentrability, RAPPEL achieves PAC/error guarantees that are never worse than strong offline-only guarantees and can improve on them, while HYRULE achieves regret guarantees that are never worse than minimax-optimal online-only guarantees and can improve on them when offline data is useful. The paper also provides experiments on a scaled-down Tetris environment intended to illustrate empirical benefits of both approaches.
strengths: Addresses an important and timely question in hybrid RL: whether one can provably improve over offline-only and online-only sample complexity barriers in linear MDPs without single-policy concentrability.
Covers both major hybrid RL paradigms in one paper: online-to-offline PAC learning and offline-to-online regret minimization.

The algorithms are conceptually natural combinations of strong existing ingredients (OPTCOV, pessimistic offline RL, LSVI-UCB++), and the claimed guarantees are computationally efficient for finite action spaces.
The partition-based analysis using offline-covered and online-explored subspaces is interesting and potentially useful beyond this paper.
Theoretical comparisons to prior hybrid RL work are extensive, and the paper clearly positions itself relative to tabular and linear-MDP literature.
Empirical section, though limited, attempts to illustrate both coverage improvement and regret improvement in a nontrivial environment.
weaknesses: Several central claims appear overstated relative to the actual assumptions and bounds. In particular, the paper repeatedly claims improvements over offline-only/online-only minimax barriers, but the guarantees depend on partition quantities, burn-in conditions, and additional assumptions that may dominate in practice.

Assumption 2 is strong and insufficiently justified. Requiring finite partial coverability for any partition is a substantial structural assumption, and the claim that it is 'achievable for any linear MDP via a transformation of the features' is not convincing as stated because feature transformations can change the problem representation and may rely on data-dependent projections.

The theoretical results have very large polynomial lower bounds/burn-in requirements (e.g., Theorem 2 requires both N_on and N_off = \tilde{\Omega}(d^{13}H^{14})), which substantially weakens the practical significance of the asymptotic improvements.

The empirical evaluation is weak relative to the theoretical ambition: only one environment, small number of trials, no ablations on key theoretical quantities/partitions, and implementations substitute core components with simpler alternatives, making it hard to validate the claimed theory.
The presentation contains multiple notation inconsistencies, typographical issues, and ambiguous statements, which make the technical claims harder to verify and reduce confidence in correctness.

The paper does not provide a convincing procedure for selecting the partition or the tolerance parameter in a way aligned with the theory; for RAPPEL, the guarantee depends on a user-chosen tolerance tied to unknown structural quantities.
methodological_flaws: The claim in Lemma 1 / surrounding discussion that for any partition one has c_on(X_on) <= d_on under Assumption 2 is not self-evident from the provided text and appears too strong without careful qualification. Bounding a coverability-type coefficient purely by subspace dimension generally requires nontrivial normalization/explorability arguments; the paper's informal justification is insufficient.

The statement that Assumption 2 is 'achievable for any linear MDP via a transformation of the features that amounts to a projection onto the eigenspace corresponding to the nonzero singular values' is scientifically questionable. A data-dependent projection based on offline covariance does not imply that every partition of the transformed feature space is explorable under the MDP dynamics, nor that the resulting transformed representation preserves the claimed uniform coverability properties.

Theorem 1 claims improvement over the offline-only bound because Sigma_off^* + Sigma_on^* \succeq Sigma_off^*. While this monotonicity is true pointwise for the displayed norm expression, it does not by itself establish a meaningful sample-complexity improvement once the online exploration cost N^*(tau), burn-in conditions, and the dependence of Sigma_on^* on reward-agnostic exploration are accounted for. The paper overinterprets this matrix inequality as a barrier-breaking result.

The proof sketch for the H^3 improvement in Theorem 1 relies on a truncation argument over sets E_h(delta_h) with cardinality bounds derived from total variance, but the sketch is too coarse to justify the final dependence involving squared partition coefficients. In particular, the transition from trajectory truncation to a lower bound on min_phi phi^T Sigma_h^* phi is nontrivial and not convincingly explained.

For HYRULE, the regret theorem requires extremely large sample lower bounds (\tilde{\Omega}(d^{13}H^{14})), yet the paper still frames the result as showing practical barrier breaking. This undermines empirical validity because the asymptotic regime where the theorem applies is far from the experiments.

The regret-to-PAC conversion in Corollary 2 is stated tersely and appears to ignore constants/log factors and the fact that the output PAC policy is randomized over episode policies. The practical interpretation as learning a near-optimal deployable policy is therefore weaker than suggested.

The empirical section does not faithfully test the proposed algorithms as analyzed: RAPPEL uses LinPEVI-ADV instead of LinPEVI-ADV+ and substitutes LSVI-UCB for FORCE within OPTCOV; HYRULE uses LSVI-UCB++ 'as-is'. These substitutions weaken the connection between experiments and theory, so the empirical evidence does not validate the stated theorems.

The comparison tables and narrative emphasize improvements over prior worst-case bounds, but there is no lower bound tailored to the hybrid linear-MDP setting under the paper's exact assumptions. Thus the claim of 'tightest theoretical guarantees currently available' is plausible but not rigorously established from the presented evidence alone.
